Investing.com — Nervous investors are paying 45x to 53x earnings for the perceived safety of Walmart (NASDAQ:WMT) and Costco (NASDAQ:COST) as November's AI sell-off rattles markets, with the Nasdaq 100 erasing $2.5 trillion in market value on November 5 alone. The banks have not escaped the pressure, as lenders pull back on new AI financing amid rising scrutiny of AI-related debt. Yet JPMorgan Chase (NYSE:JPM)—America's largest bank and the No. 1 U.S. credit card issuer—has slipped 5.5% over the past week to $324.11.

The pullback leaves JPMorgan at a fraction of the multiple investors are paying for safety elsewhere, but that low multiple is the price of a balance sheet that has to carry the credit cycle. The stock trades at just 13.3 times trailing earnings with a 2.0% dividend yield, while analysts forecast 23.8% revenue growth and 20.4% EPS growth, and InvestingPro's valuation models flag it as "Undervalued" at $396.88, 22.5% above the share price. Total debt-to-capital of 59.8% and a "Fair" Financial Health score leave earnings exposed to credit-loss provisions and deposit-cost pressure as interest rates stay elevated.

Telling a bargain bank from one that is cheap for a reason is what ProPicks AI is built for. In Financial Fortresses, InvestingPro's financial-sector strategy, JPMorgan is missing from the November lineup, which skips balance-sheet-heavy money-center banks for exchanges and asset managers that collect fees without taking loan risk.

See the zero-credit-risk financial leaders Financial Fortresses holds instead: Explore the Financial Fortresses strategy on InvestingPro

The Deposit Franchise Behind 20% Returns

JPMorgan makes its money by gathering low-cost deposits at a scale no U.S. rival matches and putting them to work across lending, trading, and advice—and that deposit base is its moat. The bank holds the No. 1 share of U.S. retail deposits and ranks No. 1 in global investment banking fees, with $5.1 trillion in assets and $372 billion in stockholders' equity. The franchise is still widening: Consumer & Community Banking added 650,000 net new checking accounts in the third quarter.

Third-quarter results confirmed how broad that franchise has become. Net income reached $15.3 billion with a 20% return on tangible common equity, comfortably above the bank's 17% through-cycle target. Net interest income rose 13% year-over-year to $27.1 billion. Corporate & Investment Bank revenue surged 14% to $22.7 billion on a 49% jump in equities, and Asset & Wealth Management drew $51 billion in long-term net inflows.

Wall Street's November opened with a sharp break for technology shares. On November 3, the Nasdaq 100 slid into a correction, falling 10.4% below its October 6 peak. Economist David Rosenberg of Rosenberg Research called a correction "probably inevitable." Two days later, the slide turned into a rout that hit every major index.

The Worst Day for the Nasdaq in 19 Months

On November 5, the Nasdaq Composite fell 5.52% to 24,315.00, its deepest one-day drop in 19 months. The move confirmed a correction, leaving the index more than 10% below its October 6 record close. The S&P 500 lost 4.36% to 7,353.73, erasing about $3 trillion of market value, and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 3.44% to 51,523.06.

Chip stocks took the worst of it, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor index dropping more than 12%. Fears of tighter AI regulation after Democrats won control of Congress drove the selling. Melissa Brown, global head of investment decision research at SimCorp, said investors appeared to be recognizing that some newly elected members of Congress and governors want to slow the pace of AI development. Jed Ellerbroek, a portfolio manager at Argent Capital Management, called it "the capitulation phase for the data center capex beneficiary stocks, especially the semiconductors."

Investors looking for names the selloff pushed down can start with our list of oversold AI stocks that Wall Street analysts see rising 50% or more.

Rate-Hike Bets Add Pressure

Interest rates gave the market a second problem. The Federal Reserve raised rates in September, and Fed officials Beth Hammack of the Cleveland Fed and Thomas Barkin of the Richmond Fed hinted that more hikes could follow. Traders were already betting on another increase in December when the selloff hit.

Hotter-than-expected inflation data then strengthened those bets. By November 16, markets were fully pricing in a December hike, according to the CME FedWatch tool. Fed Chair Kevin Warsh was scheduled to speak that day, and minutes of the central bank's October meeting were due on November 18.

For readers who want the other end of the rating scale, our ranking of NYSE stocks with huge upside potential covers the names analysts like.

Rates were not the only pressure on technology shares. Ipek Ozkardeskaya, senior analyst at Swissquote, said investors who buy into a major AI public offering may sell their existing tech holdings to pay for it, which adds to the selling in a market that is already falling.

We shared the expanded list of Analysts Turned Bearish on These 10 Stocks on Wednesday here. You can find the top 5 stocks below.
